newsitem.title: UK: Former Barings boss Baker clears name with appeal.
newsitem.headline: Former Barings boss Baker clears name with appeal.

text.p: Former Barings executive Ron Baker won a long battle to clear his name after being reprimanded by British financial watchdog the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA).
Baker told Reuters he had been completely vindicated by the SFA, adding that he bore no grudges against the watchdog, which had treated him fairly.
He had already been cleared of most misconduct charges brought against him by the SFA but had received the reprimand, the lowest form of sanction available to an SFA tribunal, in November.
"By winning his appeal today, Mr Baker has successfully rebutted all the charges brought against him following the failure of Barings," SFA chairman Nick Durlacher said in a statement.

Blue-blooded British merchant bank Barings collapsed in February 1995 after Singapore-based trader Nick Leeson ran up losses totalling some 800 million pounds ($1.3 billion) through unauthorised derivatives trades, effectively breaking the bank.
Barings was bailed-out by Dutch financial giant Internationale Nederlanden Groep NV and now trades as its investment banking arm ING Barings.

While Leeson, now aged 30, was sentenced to six years in a Singapore jail for his part in Barings' downfall, the group's chairman Peter Baring and deputy chairman Andrew Tuckey escaped censure by the SFA, prompting widespread criticism of the body.
But the watchdog did bring actions against nine former Barings executives in March 1996 and the ending of the Baker case brings this chapter of the long-running saga to an end.
Baker's victory against the SFA tribunal was all the more remarkable because he represented himself against the SFA, which had hired top barrister Presily Baxendale to put its case.
Baker, a 45-year-old Australian, said after the judgement he believed the SFA system had worked well and he had been treated fairly.
"I'm very pleased with the result," he said.
But the time it had taken for the process to begin had put pressure on his family and his wife and daughter were also happy it was now over.
"This is a day on which I feel that after a long battle I have finally been able to have my point made through the system," Baker said.
He said he had missed working in the world of finance as it had been his life for a long time. Now that he had been vindicated by the industry watchdog he would begin to look for a job, he added.
But only after he had taken a holiday and had time to recover from mounting his own defence.
"This has taken up a lot of mental energy. I think its appropriate to take a break for a while."

Baker, who was head of the financial products group of Barings Investment Bank, told a parliamentary probe into the collapse of Barings a local cover-up of an alleged fraud had prevented him from doing his job properly when he assumed responsibility for Leeson's Singapore operations.
While he has been cleared by the SFA, Baker still faces the threat of a ban from Britain's Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) from being a director of any British company for up to 15 years.
The DTI said in February it would hold preliminary hearings into the nine Barings executives charged by the SFA as well as Tuckey and would set a timetable for a final hearing of the cases.

Baker and the others also face writs from accountancy firm Coopers & Lybrand in third party proceedings after it was sued by Barings administrator Ernst & Young for what is thought to be around a million pounds.
He said he was confident he would be able to address the DTI inquiry and would now be able to concentrate on this.
Baker's lawyer Lindsay Hill, a partner at London law firm Fox Williams, told Reuters others who were pursuing his client should take note of the SFA outcome and the fact Baker had cleared his name.
